title: Installing a Compiler and Building a Program
summary: Install GCC or Clang on Windows, macOS or Linux, understand the four build stages, and learn the compiler flags that catch bugs before your program runs.
introduction: A C compiler is a command-line program that turns source files into executables, and every C programmer should know how to drive one directly, even when an editor or IDE hides it. This lesson installs GCC or Clang on each major operating system, walks through preprocessing, compiling, assembling and linking one step at a time, and introduces the warning and debugging flags you should use on every build from now on.
learningObjectives: Install a C17-capable compiler on Windows, macOS or Linux
Run the preprocessing, compile, assemble and link stages individually
Use warning, standard and sanitizer flags on every build
Read a program's exit status from the shell

blocks.text: Two free compilers implement C17 completely and are used interchangeably in this tutorial: **GCC** (the GNU Compiler Collection) and **Clang** (part of the LLVM project). They accept the same command-line flags for everything covered here. Microsoft's MSVC also compiles C, but its flags differ and its C17 support arrived late, so on Windows the smoothest route is GCC through MSYS2, or GCC inside the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL).

rows: `xcode-select --install` (installs Apple Clang; the `gcc` command runs Clang)
Install Ubuntu from the Microsoft Store, then `sudo apt install build-essential`

blocks.text: Any GCC from version 8 or Clang from version 7 onwards understands `-std=c17`. For the C23 notes in later lessons you need GCC 14 or Clang 18 and the flag `-std=c23`.
The four stages of a build

`gcc hello.c -o hello` looks like one step, but the driver program runs four tools behind the scenes. You can stop after each stage and inspect the intermediate file, which is the best way to understand what `#include` really does and where linker errors come from. Use `hello.c` from the [introduction](/tutorials/c/introduction).

blocks.title: Building hello.c one stage at a time
blocks.code:
gcc -E hello.c -o hello.i   # 1. preprocess: expand #include and macros
gcc -S hello.i -o hello.s   # 2. compile: C to assembly
gcc -c hello.s -o hello.o   # 3. assemble: assembly to object code
gcc hello.o -o hello        # 4. link: object code + C library = executable
./hello

blocks.text: Open `hello.i` in an editor: your seven-line program has become several hundred lines, because the whole of `stdio.h` was pasted in. `hello.s` is readable assembly, and `hello.o` is binary machine code that cannot run yet because `printf` is still only a name. The linker resolves that name against the C standard library and produces the executable. In day-to-day work you only use two forms: `-c` to produce an object file, and the full command without `-c` to produce a program.

By default the compiler is quiet and permissive. The flags below make it strict, and strictness is free bug-finding. The table lists the ones that matter at this stage; the full command used throughout the tutorial is `gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 file.c -o program`.

rows: Turns on the most useful warnings: unused variables, missing return values, suspicious comparisons
Adds more, including unused parameters and signed/unsigned comparisons
Compile against the C17 standard; `-std=c23` selects C23 on GCC 14+ and Clang 18+
Warn about GCC and Clang extensions that another compiler might reject
Include debugging information for `gdb`, `lldb` and the sanitizers
Optimise for speed; leave it off (the default `-O0`) while debugging
Name the output file; without it you get `a.out` (or `a.exe` on Windows)
Add run-time checks for memory errors and undefined behaviour

blocks.text: Here is a warning in action. The program compiles and runs, but the compiler tells you about a variable that is never used, which in a larger program is often the sign of a logic error.

blocks.title: unused.c
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 unused.c -o unused
unused.c: In function 'main':
unused.c:5:9: warning: unused variable 'unused' [-Wunused-variable]
    5 |     int unused = 42;
      |         ^~~~~~
$ ./unused
count = 3

blocks.text: Notice that `main` has no `return` statement. Since C99, reaching the closing brace of `main` returns 0 automatically; `main` is the only function with that privilege, and most style guides still write the `return 0;` explicitly.

The value returned from `main` is the program's **exit status**. Shell scripts, build tools and continuous-integration systems use it to decide whether a step succeeded: 0 means success, anything else means failure. In Bash and zsh the status of the last command is in `$?`; in PowerShell it is `$LASTEXITCODE`. Error messages belong on the standard error stream, `stderr`, so that they are kept apart from normal output.

blocks.title: status.c
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 status.c -o status
$ ./status
status: nothing to process
$ echo $?
2

blocks.title: Common mistake: compiling without warnings
blocks.text: A plain `gcc hello.c` compiles with almost no diagnostics and names the result `a.out`. Beginners then spend hours on bugs that `-Wall -Wextra` would have pointed at in a second, such as a variable used before it is given a value. Make the full command a habit, or put it in a shell alias or a Makefile, which is covered in [Headers and Multi-file Programs](/tutorials/c/headers-multifile).

blocks.title: Running programs on Windows
blocks.text: On Windows the output file is `hello.exe` and you run it as `.\hello` in PowerShell or `hello` in cmd. Inside an MSYS2 or WSL shell, `./hello` works exactly as on Linux.

blocks.title: Editor setup
blocks.text: Any text editor works, but [Visual Studio Code](/tutorials/vscode) with the C/C++ or clangd extension gives you inline error squiggles, auto-completion and a debugger front end. Keep compiling from the terminal as well, so that you always know what the editor is doing for you.

questions.question: Which flag makes the compiler stop after producing an object file instead of linking?
questions.explanation: `-c` compiles and assembles but does not link, producing a `.o` file. `-o` only names the output and `-S` stops after producing assembly.

questions.question: `-Wall` enables every warning the compiler is capable of producing.
questions.explanation: Despite its name, `-Wall` enables a curated set of common warnings. `-Wextra` adds more, and many specific warnings must still be requested individually.
